transcript: We've had dueling Gatsby's, dueling Romeo and Juliet, and now, perhaps the strangest of all, we have dueling shows about the Gwyneth Paltrow ski trial. That's right. This year at the Edinburgh Fringe, we have not one, but two shows based on the Gwyneth Paltrow ski trial, one of which is a musical, the other is a play with music. So completely different. I actually saw them both back to back, and while I did enjoy elements of both of them, neither of them really sold me on the concept. Which is to say, in both cases, you could definitely feel them scraping the bottom of the barrel to try and stretch out this story to a full 60 minute show. The musical only focuses on the trial and specifically focuses in on the relationship between the prosecuting attorney and Gwyneth herself. The music is very fun and the vocals are insane. They actually got Diana Vickers to play Gwyneth, who I did not know who she was, but apparently she's a big deal in the UK and was on the X Factor. But overall, the humor in this one just felt very safe. It felt like they were just going down a checklist of all of the iconic moments in the trial, and that was kind of it. Whereas in contrast, I felt like the play actually took a lot more big swings with its humor. It actually chooses to dedicate the first half to the incident itself. And The second half to the trial. This is only a two person show, so they get really creative in how they can bring in some of the side characters. Several of the characters are played by audience members reading off of a teleprompter. One of the characters is played by a puppet, and one of the characters is even played by an actual piece of fruit. And so the way that they chose to tell this story just felt a little bit more innovative to me than the musical. And the humor, even though it didn't always land, just felt a little bit wittier. And so you kind of have two imperfect shows. On one hand, you have a musical that is very polished but very safe, and on the other hand, you have a play that feels a little bit less polished but is taking bigger swings. And because of that, I wouldn't really call either a must see. it is really cool to see two takes on the same cultural phenomenon. And a lot of my personal enjoyment came from comparing the two and seeing which jokes they both made, which jokes they made differently, and which were more successful. It really is a fascinating look into the art of adaptation.
